This paper presents a comparative analysis of several machine learning models for forecasting non-performing loans in a commercial bank setting. Our research is grounded in data collected from a Bulgarian commercial bank and is subject to regulatory oversight. A total of 658,000 observations spanning six years were analyzed, with the outcome assessed based on the bank's credit policy rather than actual loan defaults. Our findings indicate that, while accurate, forecasting non-performing loans is a more complex task compared to forecasting portfolio risk. A gradient boosting model yielded the highest performance in predicting non-performing loans, surpassing decision trees and supporting the notion that forecasting portfolio risk is a more comprehensive approach. Notably, our results show that a simplified approach to forecasting non-performing loans produces comparable outcomes to the more complex gradient boosting model. Consequently, forecasting portfolio risk appears to be an effective solution for predicting both non-performing loans and credit risk in general. Our research suggests that machine learning models can be a valuable supplement to traditional statistical methods for forecasting non-performing loans. Our findings are set to contribute to ongoing discussions within the European Banking Authority regarding the use of machine learning models for forecasting and estimating capital requirements for credit risk. Our research is also expected to inform regulatory decisions regarding the use of internal rating models and floor values for estimating capital requirements. To achieve this, we first apply the membrane paradigm to express the black-hole geometry in terms of a boundary fluid description. Subsequently, we develop an action for the boundary fluid using fluid-gravity correspondence and apply it to compute quantum $S$-matrices at various punctures. Notably, our results reveal that the quantum $S$-matrices exhibit symmetry under permutation of Hecke transformations at all orders, which may have implications for information propagation in these theories. Finally, we discuss how these findings may be linked to the central charge of two-dimensional conformal theories obtained from the flow of gravity to a conformal field theory. To improve the transparency of recommender systems, post-hoc explanations have gained popularity. Users receive explanations for why certain items were recommended over others. While increasing user understanding, we've found that these explanations can weaken the models they're built on. This might happen because an overly reliant model puts too much faith in its own justifications, becoming less effective. To counter this, we've developed a method to keep the model's confidence low. Through our tests on real-world datasets, we've seen that models using our approach perform better than those without, especially in scenarios where users rely heavily on explanations to make sense of the recommendations. This suggests that lower-confidence models are more resilient to changes in user behavior. Our study highlights the trade-offs of relying on post-hoc explanations and provides guidance on balancing model accuracy with user understanding. This could help researchers and practitioners decide how much to prioritize explanations in recommender systems. Ultimately, we've made a new model available for testing, along with a dataset that shows how adjusting the model's reliance on explanations impacts its performance. Our work is now open to feedback and future investigation. This research has been accepted at WSDM'23. A pre-print version can be found at arXiv:2211.09423. We investigate the electronic properties of a two-dimensional electron system fabricated within a narrow quantum well formed by combining GaAs quantum wells and InAlAs capping layers, utilizing a unique technique that employs electron beam induced current to guide fabrication and control of electron accumulation. By examining various heterostructures with distinct surface and sub-surface potential profiles, we are able to study the influence of the surface and a specifically designed sub-surface trap layer on the 2D electron system. These sub-surface features are found to have a minimal impact on the 2D electron system's energy levels, but a noticeable effect on the work function, causing the surface Fermi level to shift by up to 0.2 eV. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the surface and sub-surface regions host distinct, spatially localized one-dimensional channels for transport. These channels, controlled by adjusting the width of the InAlAs layer, can either facilitate or impede electron flow, offering a versatile means to manipulate device behavior. By leveraging these properties, we successfully created a range of devices, including an InAs nanowire-based tunneling diode and an FET, which leverages both the 2D electron system and the unique properties of the sub-surface channel to achieve enhanced performance. These advancements have the potential to further increase device performance, enabling the creation of ultra-low power FETs. In the context of distribution-free robust learning, we investigate whether there can be a significant difference in performance between the empirical risk minimimum and the optimal risk when the sample size is sufficiently large.  We can distinguish between two main scenarios: one where the robust empirical risk converges to the optimal risk at the same rate as the standard empirical risk, and another where the convergence rate remains unchanged.  By examining specific hypothesis classes and using a combination of non-asymptotic and asymptotic analysis, we demonstrate that different scenarios can arise depending on the size of the query radius.  In particular, we show that for certain classes of halfspaces, there can be a significant gap between the empirical risk minimimum and the optimal risk when the sample size is sufficiently large, provided that the query radius exceeds a certain threshold.  This threshold is roughly proportional to the inverse of the square root of the sample size and decreases as the sample size increases.  By contrast, we also establish that for another class of halfspaces, there can be no such gap, regardless of the value of the query radius.  Our findings have significant implications for distribution-free robust learning, particularly in the context of supervised learning where the query radius is effectively the margin between classes.  We can interpret our results as suggesting that distribution-free robust learning may be possible at essentially the same cost as standard learning when the query radius exceeds a certain threshold, which is roughly proportional to the sample size. AU Mic b, a hot Jupiter orbiting its host star, experiences stellar flares that potentially influence the exoplanet's mass loss.  We analyzed AU Mic using TESS data to determine if its variability is consistent with X-ray emission from a magnetically active star, and found that its light curves can be modeled using an empirical power law with a decay time similar to that of other young stars.  We used the disc-free X-ray flux of the star as a proxy for its activity level to establish a mass loss rate for the exoplanet, and found it to be 0.00012-0.00025 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ during quiescent periods and 0.0005-0.001 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ during flares.  We also calculated the mass loss rate as a fraction of the exoplanet's mass, and found it to be 0.0003-0.6% and 1.8-3.6% during quiescent and flares periods respectively.  We compared this rate to the exoplanet's mass loss rate due to tidal forces, and found it to be significantly lower, indicating that tidal forces dominate the exoplanet's mass loss.  We also used the exoplanet's mass loss rate and a model of its atmospheric evolution to establish a lower bound for its atmospheric scale height, and found it to be 1.6 R$_\odot$. We also used the exoplanet's mass loss rate and a model of its atmospheric evolution to establish a lower bound for its atmospheric temperature, and found it to be 600 K. This research aims to assess the precision of robotic ultrasound for measuring
curvature in the spine of scoliosis patients. To evaluate this, we collected and
analyzed 3D point cloud data from X-rays and ultrasound scans on 20 patients,
focusing on 12 vertebral levels. We calculated and compared the curvature in the
spine from both types of scans. The results showed that while there was some
disagreement between the measurements, they were generally highly correlated. 
The most noticeable discrepancy occurred when the curvature was steepest. 
Notably, the agreement improved when the curvature was taken as a continuous
value along the spine rather than as individual measurements at specific
points. Based on these findings, we can conclude that while some inaccuracies are
present in the measurements, they are generally reliable and can be used to
estimate the curvature in the spine. This could potentially lead to the use of
these measurements in the determination of spinal curvature. 

Keywords: scoliosis, robotic ultrasound, spinal curvature, precision, 
determination of curvature. 

This research is a follow-up to a previous study (Nordstrom et al., 2020) and was
funded by the research grant 2018-01315 from the Swedish Research Council. 
Further details on the grant can be found at https://www.vr.se/information-en/2820/
aspx. The data collection was carried out in collaboration with the scoliosis unit
at Sahlgrenska University Hospital in Gothenburg, Sweden. The data was analyzed
using the software for analyzing ultrasound images, U-Res-Net, which was
developed in-house. The work was completed in 2020.

In hothouse climates with low-pressure systems, precipitation and cloud cover are
greatly influenced by lower atmospheric layers that utilize greenhouse gases like CO2.
This study examines the effects of radiative heating in these layers on atmospheric
circulation patterns, focusing on hothouse climates characterized by strong stationary
waves and multiple-cut jet streams. We find that reducing CO2 concentrations leads
to a significant decline in low-latitude precipitation, counterintuitive to expectations.
This outcome is caused by low-level atmospheric circulation responses to changes in
radiative heating that result in a more pronounced precipitation shield at low
latitudes, rather than the typical shift occurring at higher latitudes around the
polar front. This phenomenon highlights the importance of low-latitude atmospheric
responses to radiative forcing in shaping the climate patterns of hothouse Earth
scenarios, potentially leading to more severe and unpredictable consequences.

Deep neural networks are highly efficient at image recognition but can make mistakes when their inputs are unclear or contain noise. To counter this, researchers have developed methods that can filter out noisy data from training datasets, improving network performance. However, existing solutions are often complex and require a detailed understanding of the data distribution for effective dataset cleaning. This paper proposes a new approach called the Bayesian statistics guided label refurbishment mechanism (BLRM) to eliminate noisy labels using a simple model that can estimate the reliability of each data label. BLRM was tested on several noisy data scenarios and compared to existing methods on multiple benchmarks. The results show that BBLRM outperforms other methods, achieves better network reliability with fewer data inputs, and provides more accurate noise masks without retraining the network. Additionally, BLRM's ability to dynamically adjust label quality based on its estimates allows for more flexible and adaptive dataset cleaning compared to other methods. A novel numerical approach has been developed for describing the movement of fluid near a solid wall, by modifying the existing $\delta$-function method. This modification involves introducing a specific mathematical expression, known as the hairpin packet, which accurately represents the primary organizational unit of turbulence as identified by experimental and numerical studies. By incorporating this expression into the $\delta$$^n$-function method, the new approach, dubbed the hairpin packet representation, has been shown to outperform the original method in simulating certain aspects of turbulent flow, particularly in estimating the rate of energy dissipation. This improved performance extends to more complex turbulent regimes, suggesting that the new approach has significant potential for use in turbulence modeling. Furthermore, the new method reveals a non-random, or quasi-deterministic, nature of turbulence at intermediate Reynolds numbers, which was not captured by the original method. Overall, the results indicate that the new approach provides a more accurate and physically meaningful understanding of turbulent flows. This research aims to contribute to the development of a universal turbulence model that can be applied across a wide range of Reynolds numbers. It is envisioned that the hairpin packet can be used as a fundamental unit to build a universal turbulence model, which will be explored in future research. The widespread use of deep neural networks (DNNs) has led to significant interest in their performance under different data distributions. However, there's a lack of comprehensive studies examining how these networks handle class imbalance issues, particularly in practical real-world applications. In this research, we investigate the effects of class imbalance on K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machines, and DNNs, using a simple yet effective resampling method to analyze these impacts. Our findings reveal that while DNNs are highly resilient to class imbalance, conventional classifiers are severely affected. Moreover, our results show that oversampling improves the robustness of conventional classifiers, reducing the performance disparities between them and DNNs. Ultimately, our study highlights the need for further research into how machine learning algorithms handle and adapt to class imbalance under various data distributions. By leveraging FMM to bypass O(N^2) interactions, our code efficiently handles up to N ≈ 10^7 grid points, enabling more flexible high-resolution regions and larger far-field domains than traditional mesh-based methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our code through various test cases, including: (1) evaluating FMM's performance against exact results for 10^7 particles; (2) comparing it to a tree-based code for 10^7 grid cells; (3) simulating the final stages of a black hole merger with 2.5 million grid cells; (4) adapting it for 3D moving-body simulations; and (5) efficiently solving the Einstein equations for 10^7 grid cells in a far-field astrophysical context, all while achieving high accuracy with the FMM method. This code will soon support adaptive gravitational wave stencils, enabling more efficient computations, and is set to become a valuable tool for a range of gravitational physics research, including first-generation simulations of cosmic strings, supplementary wave propagation, and advanced gravitational dynamics. We establish a hyperbolic metric on the tangent space of the K3 surface's automorphism group, consisting of origin and origin-mapping elements. Additionally, we define a subgroup comprising hypergeometric elements derived from Galois orbits of torsion-free reflexive lattices, which can be represented in the Hermitian symmetric space of type IV. Focusing on specific reflexive lattices, we calculate the hyperbolic metric on their associated tangent spaces and demonstrate that the subgroup's geometry is defined by a right-angled Coxeter system determined by the lattice's intersection lattice. Moreover, we confirm that certain orbifolds within the Hermitian symmetric space of type IV are hyperbolic. Our findings also yield new K3 surface automorphisms of infinite order, as well as provide a new explanation for the generation of their Galois orbits. Lastly, we outline potential applications in number theory. This research is inspired by the eighth problem of the ICM 2022, specifically question 8c. Stochastic optimization in modern federated learning occurs over multiple communication rounds. Each round typically involves distributing a shared aggregate over scattered data samples, prompting participants to calculate a derived value. Current methods aim to minimize overall communication by optimizing aggregate transmission, yet they often require extensive coordination, substantial memory usage, and can be vulnerable to data distribution biases. This paper proposes an alternative framework, focusing on optimizing local computations to decrease overall communication. We introduce an optimization problem, encode it in a factor graph, and use message passing algorithms to generate structured codes capable of withstanding noisy channels. Our results demonstrate that these codes yield significant benefits in terms of weight precision. Moreover, the proposed codes require minimal storage, can be transmitted quickly, and are resilient to noisy environments, making them suitable for use in challenging stochastic optimization scenarios. Our methods are validated through extensive experiments on clustering, logistic regression, and distributed support vector machine applications. These experiments show that our codes achieve superior performance and offer a practical solution to the trade-off between communication efficiency and computation efficiency in stochastic optimization. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexey-alexandrović/structured-encoding. We explore under which conditions a graph with a specified number of vertices can be fully connected in a line. Our research focuses on identifying graphs with this capability, particularly those with the fewest possible vertices, and relates it to the independence number of these graphs, which represents the maximum number of vertices that can exist without any connected vertices to them. Our investigation into the minimum vertex count required for pancyclic graphs led us to several key findings, including the realisation that for graphs with a diameter of 2, the minimum required vertices is equal to the independence number. Additionally, we discovered that for general graphs with a diameter of d, the minimum required vertices is bounded by the sum of the independence number and d minus 2, and presented examples that match this bound. Furthermore, we established that for graphs with a diameter of 2 and a specified number of vertices, the ability to form cycles of a specified length is equivalent to the existence of a particular structure, which we then used to derive a limit on the size of cycles in graphs with a specified number of vertices and a weakly pancyclic property. Our research also allowed us to derive a limit on the size of cycles in specific types of graphs with a specified number of vertices and a pancyclic property, and presented examples that matched this bound. Finally, we identified the smallest possible values for the size of specific types of cycles in particular graphs with a specified number of vertices and a pancyclic property. Additionally, FSMSN successfully simulates interactions between shock waves and moving surfaces, aligning with theoretical predictions. transportation, energy, water, and waste management, which are crucial for a
livable and sustainable urban environment. These underground networks have
historical roots dating back to pre-existing road patterns, which are now often
incompatible with modern urban development plans. Consequently, there is a
growing need to coordinate and manage these interconnected infrastructure systems
efficiently. Currently, urban planners lack a comprehensive and reliable
decision-making framework to effectively design and manage these interconnected
infrastructure systems, which are essential for a livable and sustainable urban
environment.

This study proposes the GUIDES framework to address this challenge. It utilizes
existing urban models to integrate and synchronize the timing of underground
infrastructure projects, which are typically decided upon by regional and local
authorities. The GUIDES framework is designed to support decision makers in
their efforts to ensure that these projects align with urban development plans,
minimize costs, and maintain a sustainable balance between infrastructure
development and urban growth.

The GUIDES framework is built upon an integrated model of urban systems,
combining temporal logic-based rules with agent-based decision making to
simulate the behavior of individual GUIDES agents. Each agent represents a
specific underground infrastructure system, which is responsible for ensuring
that its actions comply with urban development rules and regulations. This
framework enables decision makers to analyze the consequences of various policy
scenarios on urban development through multi-objective optimization techniques.

and land density.

The ferroelectric phase transition in ammonium sulfate is investigated through calorimetry and dynamic light scattering.  Observations indicate that the entropy associated with this phase transition primarily originates from configurational movements of the ammonium ions, rather than from dipole correlations.  Furthermore, the presence of substantial entropy at the phase transition temperature is attributed to dynamic ion migration.  Light scattering data reveals that ion transport is linked to a correlated movement of ions, observed throughout the phase transition regime.  Ultimately, the large entropy change is found to result from the disorder introduced by this ionic migration.  This disorder is found to be enhanced by the presence of defects, such as ammonium ion vacancies, which facilitate ion transport and account for the observed entropy.  The combined analysis of acoustic and light scattering data provides insight into the disordering effect of defects on the crystal structure.  Ultimately, the disorder introduced by these defects is found to dominate the entropy change associated with the phase transition.  This is a unique example of a phase transition where the primary mechanism of entropy change can be switched between lattice and ionic degrees of freedom.  This is due to the fact that the ammonium ions can be either part of the lattice or be free to move, depending on the presence or absence of these defects. Quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality, driven by the PBR theorem, have researchers exploring new ways to quantify these phenomena. A novel framework is introduced to study these effects, utilising invariants to identify common patterns among different quantum states. This approach demonstrates that various quantum configurations can exhibit complete contextuality and nonlocality, as seen in the PBR scenario. Moreover, it reveals a profound connection between local measurements and these effects, showing that nonlocality and contextuality reduce to a single, measurable concept - the distillable contextuality. This framework provides a deeper understanding of these effects and their relationship to entanglement. Interestingly, distillable contextuality can be quantified using only a portion of the PBR resources, indicating a potential method to experimentally detect these phenomena with reduced requirements. Finally, distillable contextuality is found to be a key feature of quantum mechanics' nonlocal effects, distinct from classical systems. This research paves the way for further research into the interface of quantum nonlocality and contextuality with entanglement. We introduce HiTMap, a new approach to 3D topological navigation mapping that prioritizes efficiency and flexibility. In contrast to traditional global metric maps, HiTMap focuses on creating a more lightweight and adaptive representation for navigation. By incorporating a hierarchical data structure, HiTMap effectively balances the detailed metric information of near objects with the coarser topological characteristics of distant locations. This is achieved through the integration of a 3D Delaunay triangulation with a topological map, represented as an event list and a position map. As a result, HiTMap offers enhanced scalability, improved temporal consistency, and reduced computational and memory burdens. A real-world navigation dataset is used to evaluate the efficacy of HiTMap, demonstrating its ability to maintain both metric and topological accuracy, and resulting in a more streamlined and adaptive navigation system with a 40% reduction in computational cost and 85% less memory usage, all while achieving a 95% topological metric accuracy. Furthermore, HiTMap is shown to surpass existing methods in both efficiency and adaptability, and can be effectively utilized in a variety of navigation applications, including autonomous robotics and human navigation systems. Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have led to improved performance on tasks involving Electronic Health Records (EHRs), and heterogeneous graph neural networks have further enhanced this progress by modeling relationships between different data types. To address this limitation, we introduce a new method for unsupervised patient representation learning that leverages rich but unstructured EHR data. This approach involves a dual self-supervised framework consisting of two components: the first uses node-level self-supervision to learn representations for a single patient, and the second employs graph-level self-supervision to learn representations that capture relationships between patients. Our novel technique for self-supervised learning on heterogeneous graphs involves creating artificial labels based on observed data patterns, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on two real-world datasets, achieving comparable results to supervised learning in patient similarity tasks and outperforming existing methods in patient representation learning in clustering and anomaly detection tasks. Deep Neural Networks are highly effective in various computer vision tasks, yet they are susceptible to manipulations by malicious entities. Adversarial examples, crafted to deceive DNNs, pose a threat to a range of applications. Research has focused on developing countermeasures against these attacks, with a recent emphasis on using Generative Adversarial Networks. By creating noise that can counteract adversarial attacks, while being trained to avoid being generated by the same network that carries out the attacks, GAN-based solutions aim to neutralize such threats. Although initial studies indicated a connection between adversarial attacks and GAN stability, and proposed methods to mitigate them, they were limited to specific attack techniques and didn't generalize well. This led to a need for a more effective approach that could counter a range of attacks, with improved transferability and resistance, without relying on a prior understanding of adversarial examples. A widely accepted approach to segmenting multiple sclerosis lesions in MRI scans involves experience replay, where a pre-trained network generates heatmaps of lesions in new data, which are then refined through a maximum likelihood estimation process. In our study, we evaluated the performance of this approach when applied to MRI scans from a single hospital compared to those from multiple institutions. Our results indicate that experience replay is less effective when applied to data from different sources, leading to the proposal of a new method that combines the benefits of experience replay and semi-supervised learning to improve the segmentation of MS lesions in MRI scans. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance than existing techniques, particularly in the analysis of data from multiple institutions. Our findings suggest that experience replay can segment MS lesions in MRI scans from a single hospital more effectively than models trained from scratch, highlighting its potential as an efficient and cost-effective solution for MS lesion segmentation. We found that massive stars tend to have higher mass-to-volume ratios than star-forming regions, and that most of their mass is concentrated in smaller areas.  In contrast, regions that give rise to new stars have more diffuse mass distributions and lower mass-to-volume ratios. Initial findings reveal that a specific range of language models can't directly 
identify negated phrases from context clues alone. 
However, we discovered that negation impacts NLI task performance differently 
depending on the type and placement of negation within a sentence structure. 
While overall accuracy remains unaffected by negations, split results show 
performance variations based on negation category and position. 
Notably, we found two types of NLI models exhibit distinct behaviors in handling 
negations - one type, including BERT, tends to do better with negations placed 
at the end of a sentence, while the other, including T5, performs better with them 
at the beginning. 
Additionally, we found that two methods of NLI model training, including training 
on paraphrased sets and using contrastive training, can mitigate performance drops 
caused by negations. 
Ultimately, our research suggests that NLI models should be evaluated under 
various negation scenarios to provide a more accurate understanding of their 
capabilities.

The standard decoder approach in neural machine translation is inefficient because it processes one target word at a time, which hinders the overall translation performance, particularly in large context scenarios. To address this issue, we suggest a new 'look-ahead' attention mechanism that allows a part of the decoder to consider look-ahead positions before computing the probability distribution of subsequent target words. To achieve this, we introduce an intermediate layer - the look-ahead representation layer - to convert look-ahead attention information into a format that can be utilized by the look-ahead attention mechanism. Empirical studies conducted on English-to-German and English-to-Russian language pairs have demonstrated the enhanced effectiveness of this proposed look-ahead attention mechanism. Additionally, our analysis of source-side and target-side attention patterns indicates that look-ahead attention can be applied in a position-dependent manner. Ultimately, we propose two distinct architectures that can incorporate the look-ahead attention mechanism in a more efficient manner. The first one involves integrating it into the affine transformation step, whereas the second one involves incorporating it into the softmax calculation. The results of our experiments have shown that these two architectures are equally effective. Finally, we have explored the potential of combining the look-ahead attention mechanism with coverage attention and monotonicity constraints, and our findings suggest that look-ahead attention can be seamlessly integrated with these methods. The source code for the proposed look-ahead attention mechanism is publicly available on the GitHub platform under the repository name 'look-ahead-attention-nmt'. The experimental data and pre-trained models used in this study can be accessed from the Turku NMT repository located at https://github.com/alvestam/ntu-nmt/tree/master/data. The paper presents the underlying research results, whereas a companion paper published at the 2022 Conference of the Association for Computational Linguistics details the implementation specifics and showcases the potential of look-ahead attention in sequence-to-sequence models. This article explores an alternative approach to symplectic geometry by focusing on the geometry of cotangent bundles, resulting in a more direct computation of curvature weights and straightforward proofs of theorems 1, 3, and 4. Additionally, this framework leads to the derivation of an explicit formula for the associated Euler calculus, and it is shown that the derived Euler calculus is isomorphic to the standard one, confirming the conjecture stated in arXiv:1808.76. However, the proof relies on the geometry of the cotangent bundle rather than the convex body theory associated with K. Strombergsson. Furthermore, the article provides explicit calculations for the Gauss curvature weights and their relation to the geometry of cotangent bundles, and it also generalizes the method to apply to other bundle projections, such as those for Lagrangian Fubini-Study manifolds, and it is noted that the case of complex projective spaces yields a known result, but the other cases remain to be verified. Lastly, the article mentions the potential for further research on the geometry of cotangent bundles, specifically in relation to the general case of Lagrangian Fubini-Strombergsson weights.

We introduce LaViSE, a novel text generator specifically designed to provide human-understandable explanations for the inner workings of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). LaViSE takes a CNN layer's learned representation and produces an interpretable text description, drawing from a language dataset pre-trained using generative adversarial networks. LaViSE's architecture combines a word embedding module that maps concept latents to words, with a concept embedding module that predicts the concept latents from the CNN layer's learned representation. These modules are trained in an adversarial setup where accuracy is measured by both numerical and semantic similarity. We evaluate LaViSE's performance on multiple tasks and networks, showing that it can generate accurate, semantically sound text descriptions for complex CNN architectures like ResNet-50 and Vision Transformer. Notably, LaViSE's text explanations for two specific networks, Inception-ResNet-A and ResNet-50, significantly align with the corresponding network design principles, as identified by a large knowledge base. This study contributes to the understanding of deep learning models by generating human-readable explanations. We release LaViSE's source code and dataset on GitHub under an open-source license. In contrast, Singular ARMA models fill this gap by inhering the capabilities of both High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor and Singular Regression models. We provide an in-depth analysis of Singular ARMA models, covering their mathematical representation, statistical inference methods, and applications in forecasting. We derive key findings regarding the model's identification, statistical inference, and forecasting methods, and prove that these can be efficiently computed using principal component analysis and vector autoregression techniques. We demonstrate the model's utility through a study on forecasting US inflation. We compare the forecasting performance of Singular ARMA models with other conventional models, such as the vector autoregression model, through an analysis of various specifications of the number of factors and orders of ARMA. The results show that Singular ARMA models can effectively capture the underlying patterns of the data and provide accurate multi-step forecasts. In particular, models with one factor and order 1 or 2 tend to perform the best. We verify that the model's parameters converge at a rate of n/(m+1) for both inference and forecasting, and that the model's forecast is within the confidence interval derived from bootstrapping. The findings show that Singular ARMA models can be a reliable choice for forecasting the future values of multivariate time series data. In addition, we suggest using the model's forecast as the base forecast and combining it with other methods, such as bagging and boosting, to enhance the model's forecasting performance. Deep learning models are increasingly being used in safety-critical applications, such as autonomous driving, despite concerns about their reliability. These concerns stem from the models' limitations in capturing the underlying data distribution, leading to unpredictable behavior when encountering novel situations. To address this issue, we propose a Bayesian approach for assessing the constraints of a predictive deep learning model, leveraging uncertainty quantification to identify and mitigate potential errors. By applying this approach to a real-world self-driving car scenario, we successfully developed a safer-based system that integrates uncertainty quantification, mitigating a critical bug in the model caused by overconfident predictions. Our findings highlight the value of combining safer-based system techniques with Bayesian methods to enhance AI system reliability. By taking into account the statistical properties of magnetic fields and scalars in turbulent flows, it is possible to derive new expressions for angular momentum transport and other relevant processes, which can then be used to model more complex dynamo processes. This approach has the potential to lead to new insights into the mechanisms of solar and stellar magnetism, particularly in terms of how small-scale turbulent effects on magnetic fields can influence large-scale magnetic field development. By analyzing the properties of turbulent flows and their impact on magnetic fields, it may be possible to gain a deeper understanding of the origins of solar and stellar magnetic fields, and to develop more accurate models of these complex astrophysical systems. This paper proposes a new utility function for an investor with an uncertain lifetime. Recent Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG) models combine a dense retriever and a sequence generator, trained end-to-end on a joint model. To adapt these models to new tasks, fine-tuning is a viable option, but presents unique challenges. Specifically, the need to balance updates between the retriever and generator components, to avoid disrupting dense retriever performance, and to prevent information loss. This study investigates the effectiveness of fine-tuning RAG models using different approaches, including in-vitro and in-vivo methods, which involve updating only the generator or entire model, respectively. The in-vivo methods examined include full end-to-end fine-tuning, and fine-tuning the generative component alone, while the dense retriever is frozen. To assess the impact of fine-tuning on dense retriever performance, retrieval-based loss is introduced, and the need to retrain the dense retriever after fine-tuning is also explored. The evaluation of fine-tuning RAG models on question answering and document question answering tasks suggests that in-vivo methods yield better results, and that end-to-end fine-tuning performs similarly to fine-tuning the generative component alone. Moreover, incorporating a retrieval-based loss during fine-tuning helps to mitigate degradation of dense retriever performance. Finally, retraining the dense retriever after fine-tuning is found to improve overall performance, and to be particularly beneficial when the generative component alone was fine-tuned. These findings provide insights for fine-tuning RAG models in practice. The code and pre-trained models used in this study are available at https://github.com/alevshin/fine-tuning-rag. The study also highlights the need for further research on adapting dense retrievers to new tasks, and to explore alternative fine-tuning methods that balance updates between the dense retriever and generative components. To address this gap, a new method, named generative-dense transferable objectives (GDTO), is proposed, which involves fine-tuning the dense and generative components in parallel, using a shared objective that combines dense and generative losses. The results show that GDTO yields better results, and can be used as an alternative to existing fine-tuning methods. The study also demonstrates that incorporating pre-trained knowledge from other dense models can further improve fine-tuning outcomes. Specifically, a new method, named knowledge distillation, is proposed, which involves fine-tuning the dense and generative components, while imposing soft constraints derived from a pre-trained dense model. We introduce a novel graph-based method that leverages photometric information to
enhance the process of identifying matching sources across disparate catalogs.
Notably, our approach yields a 50% increase in the precision of matching results,

underlying technique can be viewed as an extension of the standard spatial
matching algorithm. Furthermore, we illustrate how our method can effectively
handle datasets of varying scales, including both small and large datasets.
Moreover, we provide a theoretical analysis of the computational complexity,
demonstrating a logarithmic scaling of running time with the number of sources.
Lastly, we discuss potential avenues for further research and the integration of
additional metadata. Experimental results are presented in Section 6.

Recent research indicates that large pre-trained language models can excel at complex tasks after specialized training, yet their effectiveness and efficiency are often unclear. To address this, we investigated the performance of six different models, including pre-trained and fine-tuned options, for the task of grading essays in English. We considered models of varying sizes, training approaches, and optimization techniques, as well as different data sets to assess their task-specific adaptability. Our findings suggest that a well-fine-tuned model with a relatively modest number of parameters (around 55 million) can match or even surpass the performance of larger pre-trained models like T5 or FLAN with hundreds of millions of parameters in tasks such as essay scoring. Notably, our results show that a pre-trained BART model with active learning can achieve the best overall performance, even using a relatively small subset (10% of the total) of the data for training. Our study highlights the potential for task-specific models with a more modest number of parameters to achieve comparable or even superior performance when it comes to complex language tasks such as essay scoring. Additionally, our research suggests that active learning can be an effective strategy to achieve high performance in such tasks by utilizing a smaller, more representative sample of the data. Overall, our findings underscore the importance of carefully evaluating and comparing different models to optimize their performance and efficiency for specific tasks. As such models continue to evolve, our research provides insights into the potential for further improvement in task-specific models to facilitate better decision-making and resource allocation in education settings. A common issue in active learning is the time-consuming process of manually labeling instances. To optimize this process, researchers have developed methods to automatically select the most relevant instances to be labeled by experts. This paper focuses on a specific aspect of this problem - how to effectively use the limited capacity of expert validators. To address this challenge, we propose two solutions. Firstly, we suggest transforming the problem of suppressing false positives into a ranking task and reorganizing the models' ranking list using the top validated instances. This strategy allows existing machine learning-based validators can be leveraged without additional supervision. Secondly, we developed a new unsupervised validator that dynamically adjusts its validation threshold to validate only a specified proportion of instances. This approach is inspired by the strategy employed by human validators, who often establish a balance between validating all instances and missing relevant information. To evaluate our method, we conducted a series of experiments on various datasets and learning setups, comparing it with existing time-consuming methods. The results show that our approach significantly reduces the total time required to achieve a specific accuracy level. To facilitate the reproduction of our results, we have made our code available online. This paper presents new insights into the optimization of expert validators' capacity and offers a practical solution to this complex problem. The proposed method can be applied to any dataset and algorithm, and its impact is particularly noticeable in scenarios where data is scarce and labeling time is critical. The findings also highlight the importance of considering the interplay between active learning and validation in the context of deep learning models. We discovered that both the overall style and hand-specific details of these animations matter, and we were able to quantify how different style factors contribute to their realism. This research focuses on refining the asymptotic representation of the eikonal equation for geometrical optics with compact support potentials. By enhancing the asymptotic relations, we derive more accurate estimates for the remainders, which we apply to obtain improved estimates for scattering phase shifts and cross sections. These findings are particularly useful for potentials with certain geometric characteristics, such as being strictly convex. Beyond the scalar case, we extend our approach to elliptic operators, achieving similar improvements in the scattering theory. This paper introduces a novel framework for semi-supervised learning, termed TransMutation, which enables targeted and flexible class label transformations during yielding unlabeled samples with alternative class labels. TransMutation encompasses two primary applications: transmutations and mixture mutations. TransMutation can apply subtle and nuanced class label transformations, suitable for datasets with a coherent and continuous label structure. In contrast, mixture mutations are designed for datasets with distinct and separate class labels, producing unlabeled samples by assigning multiple class labels to each target sample. Our research demonstrates that both transmutations and mixture mutations outperform existing semi-supervised learning methods, with mixture mutations yielding better performance than transmutation. Notably, our TransMutation framework offers enhanced control over the class label transformations produced, allowing for tailored data augmentation strategies. This is illustrated by our ability to produce targeted class label transformations, such as generating more images of patients with a specific aneurysm size. Additionally, our method can produce unlabeled samples with diverse class labels by adjusting the mixture coefficients. Our experiments show that our TransMutation framework generalizes well to real-world applications, including medical image analysis, with promising results in patient outcome prediction from magnetic resonance imaging. The vacuum fluctuations of light play a significant role in the stability of quantum systems, particularly when studying the unique characteristics that emerge at the intersection of light and matter. In this context, we investigate how the statistical properties of light are affected by the rapid relaxation of a quantum system. We focus on a setup consisting of two interconnected quantum systems within separate cavities, where one cavity is designed to trap photons at a specific energy, while the other is a highly damped quantum system interacting with it. By analyzing the rapid relaxation processes, we reveal substantial changes in the statistical properties of light, including the significant suppression of certain correlations, resulting in a shift towards Gaussian distributions. These findings are highly relevant to the study of cavity polaritons, where the rapid relaxation of states can lead to the suppression of certain low-frequency fluctuations. We further demonstrate that the rapid relaxation of states can be utilized as an effective method for generating coherent light, even when the initial system is not in a pure state. Notably, our research is grounded in the study of cavity polaritons, a field where the rapid relaxation of states can provide insights into the suppression of low-frequency fluctuations, ultimately enabling the effective method for generating coherent light, even from an initially mixed state. A novel spring-driven actuation system utilizing energy storage and conversion
is introduced to facilitate efficient actuation in dynamic walking patterns for
robots. This innovative approach eliminates the need for costly and complex
amplifiers commonly used in traditional voltage-controlled actuators, making it
suited for applications requiring high power and efficient energy usage, such
as legged locomotion. By harnessing energy from springs, the proposed system
achieves a significant reduction in the number of required actuators, thus
increasing its overall efficiency and power output capabilities. To demonstrate the
system's efficacy, a prototype robot utilizing the developed actuation was
tested using a simple control strategy based on velocity feedback, achieving a
stable and consistent gait pattern at various speeds. Furthermore, the experimental
results confirm the system's ability to maintain accurate joint positions during
motion, even when subjected to external disturbances. By integrating the proposed
actuators into robots designed for hopping and running gaits, the system's
efficiency and stability were also validated through both simulation and real-world
testing. The accompanying video at https://youtu.be/6Q8wvzrjz8A provides visual
evidence of the system's performance in both simulation and reality. This study's
findings are expected to pave the way for the development of more efficient and
powerful actuators in robots. The presented design is intended to inspire the
creation of low-cost, high-power actuators in robots, ultimately leading to
innovative applications in robots. The system's design files and source code are
available for download at https://github.com/leggedrobot/spring_actuators2022.

This paper addresses the challenge of low-level visual features extraction from images by humans, specifically in the context of fashion, to support a novel application - retrieving similar clothing items. Although advancements have been made in this area, the task of accurately identifying and categorizing clothing items remains complex and requires further refinement. To address this limitation, we propose a multi-faceted approach, combining two pre-trained convolutional neural networks to enhance feature extraction accuracy. Our approach leverages both local and global visual characteristics to develop a comprehensive set of features. Furthermore, we utilize a novel technique, called the weighted average of L2 norms, to effectively manage feature dimensionality and prioritize the most representative characteristics. Our approach demonstrates superior performance in the field of fashion instance-level image retrieval, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets.
